subject: Communication
title: The 93% Myth: Words vs. Body Language
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The 93% Myth: Words vs. Body Language.

hook.text: You've probably heard that 93% of communication is nonverbal. It's the most misquoted stat in psychology.

buildup.text: Albert Mehrabian's 1967 study tested how people interpret feelings — not all communication.

discovery.text: His 7-38-55 rule (words-tone-body) applies only when someone's words contradict their tone or expression.

twist.text: In normal conversation, words matter enormously. But when words and body clash, we believe the body.

climax.text: The real takeaway: when verbal and nonverbal signals conflict, nonverbal wins every time.

punchline.text: Body language doesn't replace words. It overrules them.

quiz.question: When does Mehrabian's 7-38-55 rule actually apply?
options: When words contradict tone or expression

details.summary: The famous claim that 93% of communication is nonverbal comes from Albert Mehrabian's 1967 studies, but it only applied to feelings and attitudes expressed through single words. Generalizing it to all communication is a widespread misquotation.
details.whyItMatters: Believing the 93% myth leads people to overvalue body language and undervalue what is actually said, distorting training programs and everyday judgments.
takeaways: Mehrabian studied feelings conveyed by single words only
The 93% figure does not apply to general conversation
Words, tone, and body language all matter in context

faq.question: What did Mehrabian's study actually measure?
faq.answer: Mehrabian tested how listeners judged a speaker's feelings when a single word was spoken with conflicting tone and facial expression. The 7-38-55 split applied only to that narrow scenario, not to everyday conversations where content carries far more weight.

faq.question: How much of communication is truly nonverbal?
faq.answer: There is no single reliable percentage. The contribution of nonverbal cues depends on context, relationship, and message type. In technical discussions words dominate, while in emotional exchanges body language carries more weight.
